RealtimeWAM: How Fast Can I Run
My World Action Model?

Huanan Liu, Ye Li, Kangye Ji, Xiaoyu Chen, Hanyun Cui, Yutian Shen
Yuan Meng, Chenglei Wu, Jingyan Jiang, Bo Li, Zhi Wang
Tsinghua University YuanxingGuangnian Robotics Nanjing University ††thanks: Work done during an internship at Tsinghua University.††thanks: Corresponding author.
Abstract

World Action Models (WAMs) combine visual dynamics modeling with action generation, but their high inference latency limits responsive robot control. Recent efforts accelerate inference by removing explicit future-video generation at test time, as in FastWAM, an approach that requires a specially tailored architectural design. More general caching strategies exploit feature redundancy, but redundancy alone does not capture the changing computational demands of closed-loop control. To address these challenges, we present RealtimeWAM, a general, training-free framework that coordinates parallel execution with adaptive computation for low-latency inference across diverse WAM architectures. We exploit layerwise dependencies to overlap observation processing with prediction. However, concurrent branches still compete for GPU resources, limiting the benefit of parallel execution. We therefore adapt computation throughout the pipeline through selective reuse, caching observation features in visually stable regions and reusing Transformer residuals while reserving additional refinement for small predicted adjustments. We evaluate RealtimeWAM on FastWAM and OpenWAM across RoboTwin, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus. On an RTX 4090, measured mean inference latencies are 24.09 and 63.09 ms, corresponding to average speedups of 8.90×\times and 10.67×\times. Average success rates are 82.75% and 87.41%, respectively, within 0.02 and 0.53 percentage points of native inference. Across five real-world tasks, RealtimeWAM improves average success rates over native inference by 17.2 and 37.2 percentage points on FastWAM and OpenWAM, respectively. Project page: https://anonymous.4open.science/w/realtimewam/.

   

1 Introduction

World Action Models (WAMs) integrate visual dynamics modeling with action generation, providing predictive representations for robotic control (Cen et al., 2025; Bi et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026). However, their substantial inference cost limits how quickly a robot can respond to changes in its environment. This limitation is particularly problematic in dynamic manipulation, where the scene continues to evolve while the model generates an action (Black et al., 2025b). For example, a moving object on a conveyor may shift away from its observed position before the predicted action is executed. Reducing latency from observation to action is therefore essential for using WAMs to control robots in real time.

Recent work has reduced inference cost through architectural simplification and computational reuse. For example, FastWAM removes future-video generation at inference while retaining joint training with video (Yuan et al., 2026), and diffusion caching methods such as TeaCache avoid repeated Transformer computation by reusing residual features (Liu et al., 2025a). These advances leave two further questions for WAM execution in real time. First, reducing computation alone does not resolve how observation processing and prediction should be scheduled under their data dependencies and shared hardware constraints. Second, caching decisions based on denoising similarity are not explicitly tied to the responsiveness and precision required by the current action. Fixed evaluation schedules likewise apply the same computational budget throughout a rollout, despite changing execution requirements. Further acceleration therefore calls for coordinating parallel execution with computation that adapts to the current observation and predicted motion.

To address these challenges, we present RealtimeWAM, a framework that coordinates parallel execution with adaptive computation for existing WAM architectures without additional training. We first exploit the layerwise dependencies between processing the current observation (Prefill) and prediction. As each layer produces the required observation features, the corresponding prediction computation can begin while Prefill continues (Figure 2). This allows Prefill to overlap with action prediction and, when present, future-video generation. However, concurrent branches compete for shared GPU compute resources, limiting the speedup achievable through overlap alone.

To ease this contention, we exploit temporal redundancy across observations to reduce the Prefill workload. Changes in the current observation guide which tokens receive fresh computation, while cached features supply the remaining positions. However, reducing the number of refreshed tokens does not always reduce latency, as different token counts can fall within the same latency plateau (Table 3, right). We use this available capacity to refresh additional tokens with larger feature changes in the first layer, limiting reuse error at little extra latency. This reuse policy accounts for hardware latency and reduces the workload competing with prediction while keeping observation features current.

Token reuse reduces the cost of the first stage, but subsequent denoising still requires repeated network evaluations. To further accelerate inference, we adapt the refresh schedule of cached Transformer residuals according to predicted motion. A coarse action prediction provides a displacement signal for deciding whether further refinement is needed. Motion amplitude and the effect of additional computation vary within an episode (Figure 3), motivating a budget adapted to motion. We allocate fewer evaluations to large predicted movements to favor rapid replanning, while retaining additional evaluations for small adjustments. We evaluate this allocation through closed-loop ablations in Section 4.4 and paired prediction comparisons in Appendix E. Refinement continues from the same initial denoising trajectory, preserving the computation already performed.

We evaluate FastWAM and OpenWAM on RoboTwin, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus. Combining execution optimizations with adaptive computation gives measured average speedups of 8.90×\times and 10.67×\times, respectively, relative to native inference. Average success rates decrease by 0.02 and 0.53 percentage points (Table 1). Controlled experiments examine which scheduling and computation allocation choices account for these gains.

Our main contributions are:

  • ∙\bullet

    We design a parallel schedule guided by layer dependencies that overlaps observation processing with action prediction and, where applicable, future-video generation.

  • ∙\bullet

    We develop a token reuse policy that reduces the Prefill workload and exploits hardware latency plateaus to refresh additional informative tokens.

  • ∙\bullet

    We adapt Transformer residual caching to predicted motion, using the displacement of a coarse action prediction to determine whether further refinement is needed.

  • ∙\bullet

    We evaluate two WAM architectures on three simulation benchmarks and five real-world tasks, with controlled experiments examining execution, token allocation, and predictive refinement.

2 Related Work

World action models and real-time inference.

Diffusion Policy and π0\pi_{0} generate actions with diffusion and flow matching, respectively (Chi et al., 2023; Black et al., 2025a). WAMs couple visual prediction with action generation (Shen et al., 2025; Bi et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a). FastWAM omits future-video generation at inference; OpenWAM jointly predicts video and actions (Yuan et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026). Flash-WAM distills joint prediction to fewer steps (Akbari et al., 2026). RTC, SmolVLA, and LingBot-VA overlap policy inference with action execution (Black et al., 2025b; Shukor et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026a). Realtime-VLA and VLA-Perf examine inference optimization (Ma et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2026). We overlap observation processing and prediction within one request.

Temporal reuse and diffusion caching.

Diffusion caching reuses or extrapolates intermediate features across timesteps (Ma et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025a; Zou et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025b). FasterCache and PAB reuse diffusion features and attention outputs (Lyu et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025); TokenCache learns token importance for selective caching (Lou et al., 2024). PostDiff compares fewer denoising steps with mixed-resolution generation and module caching (Du et al., 2025). VLA-Cache, BAC, and EfficientVLA apply reuse at visual-token, block, and diffusion-head levels (Xu et al., 2025; Ji et al., 2026a; Yang et al., 2025). Our token reuse reduces Prefill contention and uses latency plateaus to refresh additional tokens.

Adaptive computation.

DynamicViT learns token sparsification; FastV prunes visual tokens using attention scores (Rao et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2024). PRANCE jointly adapts tokens and channels (Li et al., 2026d). AdaCache uses video motion to guide caching (Kahatapitiya et al., 2025). SAG learns observation-conditioned pruning; Test-time Sparsity combines parallel inference with learned cached-feature selection (Ji et al., 2026c; Ji et al., 2026b). SP-VLA couples scheduling with token pruning; ElegantVLA allocates computation across perception, language, and action (Li et al., 2026c; Li et al., 2026b). TS-DP uses reinforcement learning to adapt speculative diffusion decoding (Li et al., 2025). RealtimeWAM allocates Prefill and refinement budgets from observation changes and predicted motion, without training a selector.

3 Method

RealtimeWAM coordinates execution order and fresh computation within each WAM request (Figure 4). We first overlap independent work using the model’s dependencies. Hardware-aware token reuse then reduces the observation workload competing with prediction, while motion-adaptive refinement allocates subsequent network evaluations.

3.1 Anatomy of WAM inference

At request tt, a WAM maps images, robot state, and an instruction to an HH-step action chunk. Current-observation processing, termed Prefill, provides features for action prediction and, when present, joint video–action prediction. Under first-frame-causal attention and fixed clean-frame conditioning, observation tokens are independent of the evolving prediction. Their keys and values (K/V) provide the observation context required by the predictive branches at each layer.

Let RtR_{t} be the observation positions refreshed after the first layer, and NtN_{t} the number of full predictive Transformer evaluations. Request latency can be decomposed as

Tt≈Tfirst​(Rt)+∑j=2NtTfull,j+Tlight+Tfinish.T_{t}\approx T_{\mathrm{first}}(R_{t})+\sum_{j=2}^{N_{t}}T_{\mathrm{full},j}+T_{\mathrm{light}}+T_{\mathrm{finish}}. (1)

The first stage includes input preparation, Prefill, and the initial prediction. Thus RtR_{t} controls the workload within the first stage, while NtN_{t} controls the amount of subsequent refinement. TlightT_{\mathrm{light}} covers the remaining input embeddings, output-head evaluations, and sampler updates; TfinishT_{\mathrm{finish}} covers final action postprocessing and return to the CPU. The measured request includes online selection, data movement, and synchronization.

3.2 Dependency-aware parallel execution

We overlap independent input preparation: VAE encoding produces visual latents while context preparation produces instruction features and conditioning K/V, reusing instruction features when unchanged.

Prediction consumes observation K/V layer by layer. We release them immediately after projection, allowing prediction to proceed alongside the remaining Prefill attention and FFN operations (Figure 2). This overlaps observation processing with the first predictive evaluation, including the future-video branch when present.

Within each layer, local projections run concurrently; joint attention waits for the required K/V, after which conditioning attention and FFNs resume. Fused operators, preallocated buffers, and CUDA Graph replay reduce transfers, repeated assembly, and launch overhead.

The overlapping branches share GPU resources, so we reduce their concurrent workload by refreshing selected observation positions and reusing cached outputs at the others.

3.3 Hardware-aware token reuse

The refresh budget must reflect observation changes and hardware cost. GPU matrix operations exhibit tile- and wave-quantization effects (NVIDIA, 2023). Profiling our concurrent first stage reveals ranges of token counts with nearly unchanged latency (Table 3, right). We treat each plateau’s upper end as an execution capacity. Figure 5 shows how RGB changes establish required updates and feature changes guide the additional updates that fill this capacity.

Selecting an execution capacity.

For MM observation tokens, let DtD_{t} contain positions whose mean absolute RGB change exceeds δ\delta. We require these positions to refresh and reserve a fraction α\alpha of the remaining positions to capture changes not identified by RGB alone. Offline profiling of the concurrent first stage gives execution capacities ℬ\mathcal{B}, including full refresh MM. We choose the smallest capacity covering the required and reserved updates:

rt=|Dt|+⌈α⁡(M−|Dt|)⌉,bt=min⁡{b∈ℬ:b≥rt}.r_{t}=|D_{t}|+\lceil\alpha(M-|D_{t}|)\rceil,\qquad b_{t}=\min\{b\in\mathcal{B}:b\geq r_{t}\}. (2)

Each capacity uses a prepared execution shape for concurrent Prefill and prediction.

Filling the selected capacity.

The full first layer provides current features for every position. To spend the remaining capacity on changing features, we rank positions outside DtD_{t} by normalized change from the preceding observation:

st,i=2​‖ft,i0−ft−1,i0‖1max⁡(‖ft,i0‖1+‖ft−1,i0‖1,ϵ),Rt=Dt∪Topbt−|Dt|⁡{st,i:i∉Dt}.s_{t,i}=\frac{2\|f^{0}_{t,i}-f^{0}_{t-1,i}\|_{1}}{\max(\|f^{0}_{t,i}\|_{1}+\|f^{0}_{t-1,i}\|_{1},\epsilon)},\qquad R_{t}=D_{t}\cup\operatorname{Top}_{b_{t}-|D_{t}|}\{s_{t,i}:i\notin D_{t}\}. (3)

Here, ft,i0f^{0}_{t,i} is the first-layer feature and Topk\operatorname{Top}_{k} returns the kk highest-scoring indices. The set RtR_{t} retains every RGB-required position and supplements it with feature-ranked positions. The same set serves subsequent layers; the feature reference advances at every observation.

Executing fresh and cached tokens.

For each reused layer ℓ>0\ell>0, selected positions update their FFN cache entries while the others retain their last computed values. Writing Φℓ\Phi_{\ell} for the FFN computation and zt,iℓz^{\ell}_{t,i} for its current input, the update is

Ct,iℓ={Φℓ​(zt,iℓ),i∈Rt,Ct−1,iℓ,i∉Rt.C^{\ell}_{t,i}=\begin{cases}\Phi_{\ell}(z^{\ell}_{t,i}),&i\in R_{t},\\ C^{\ell}_{t-1,i},&i\notin R_{t}.\end{cases} (4)

FFN reuse applies to Prefill; future-video and action tokens are fully computed at each selected evaluation. Compatible operations batch refreshed observation and prediction rows. Attention and current residual gates remain fully computed (Appendix D). Full refresh initializes the FFN cache; episode or conditioning changes invalidate incompatible history.

3.4 Motion-adaptive refinement

Repeated Transformer evaluations remain on the critical path after the first stage. We cache the input-to-output residual of the Transformer. Each denoising step embeds the current latent, adds the cached residual, and evaluates the output head with the current timestep. Full evaluations refresh this residual. Motivated by the varying precision demands in Figure 3, we use predicted motion amplitude to allocate refinement: large motions favor earlier replanning, while small adjustments receive additional computation.

Both schedules share two initial Transformer refreshes. After the second, we decode a coarse action prediction. For current end-effector position ptp_{t} and predicted physical positions p^t,k(2)\widehat{p}^{(2)}_{t,k}, we use the maximum displacement to choose the evaluation budget:

mt=max1≤k≤H∥p^t,k(2)−pt∥2,Nt=2+2 1[mt≤τ].m_{t}=\max_{1\leq k\leq H}\|\widehat{p}^{(2)}_{t,k}-p_{t}\|_{2},\qquad N_{t}=2+2\,\mathbf{1}[m_{t}\leq\tau]. (5)

The threshold τ\tau is fixed during deployment. The 2F schedule refreshes at Euler updates 0 and 3; the 4F schedule adds refreshes at 6 and 9. Both perform ten Euler updates using the current output-head prediction at each step. Refinement continues from the shared prefix with the same noise and conditioning (Figure 4c).

Together, RtR_{t} and NtN_{t} allocate fresh computation within the first stage and across later evaluations. Section 4.4 compares fixed and adaptive budgets; Appendix E gives the sampler settings and paired-output diagnostics.

4 Experiments

We evaluate RealtimeWAM on simulation and real-world manipulation tasks, and ablate execution optimizations, token reuse, and motion-adaptive refinement.

4.1 Experimental setup

Backbones, benchmarks, and baselines. We evaluate FastWAM and OpenWAM on RoboTwin 2.0 clean/randomized (Chen et al., 2025), LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023), and LIBERO-Plus (Fei et al., 2026). Each backbone’s native inference is the reference; VLA-Cache (Xu et al., 2025), TeaCache (Liu et al., 2025a), ToCa (Zou et al., 2025), and BAC (Ji et al., 2026a) provide training-free caching baselines. We enable compilation and CUDA Graph replay for the caching baselines and RealtimeWAM. Baselines retain their original execution schedules; RealtimeWAM adds the proposed parallel execution. Table 1 reports success rates per setting and equally weighted averages over the four settings. LIBERO category results appear in Appendix B.4.

Metrics and timing. We report success rate and full-request latency, with speedup relative to native inference. Runtime measurements use BF16, batch size one, and a modified 48 GiB RTX 4090. Timing covers the prepared CPU image/state interface through denormalized CPU actions, including input processing, model and sampler execution, transfers, and synchronization. Compilation, graph capture, warmup, profiling, and robot execution are excluded. 2F/4F denote two/four full Transformer evaluations within ten Euler updates. The main comparison and execution ablations report mean latencies measured during complete closed-loop rollouts. Model-specific interfaces and checks appear in Appendix C.

4.2 Overall comparison

Success–latency tradeoff. RealtimeWAM has the lowest reported average latency on both backbones (Table 1). FastWAM latency decreases from 214.33 to 24.09 ms (8.90×\times), while the success rate changes from 82.77% to 82.75%. OpenWAM latency decreases from 672.83 to 63.09 ms (10.67×\times), with the success rate changing from 87.94% to 87.41%. Relative to Native with compilation and CUDA Graph replay, speedups are 4.14×\times on FastWAM and 7.15×\times on OpenWAM (Table 9).

Comparison with caching baselines. With compilation and CUDA Graph replay, TeaCache is the fastest competing baseline at 49.28/245.99 ms on FastWAM/OpenWAM, with lower average success rates than ours on both. BAC retains a higher OpenWAM success rate (87.77% versus 87.41%) at 305.08 ms. Appendix C.3 compares original and compiled execution for each baseline.

4.3 Sources of latency reduction

Table 2 adds execution optimizations at fixed evaluation budgets: first-forward timings come from 2F runs, and complete requests from separate 10F runs. After graph replay and compilation, parallel execution reduces first-forward latency from 36.21 to 17.77 ms on FastWAM and from 60.62 to 37.12 ms on OpenWAM. Token reuse further reduces these to 17.69 and 31.62 ms; its incremental benefit is larger on OpenWAM in this configuration.

Request latency with 10F falls from 214.33 to 29.47 ms on FastWAM and 672.83 to 217.24 ms on OpenWAM, establishing execution savings before adaptive evaluation counts are introduced. Detailed stage and preparation measurements appear in Appendix C.

4.4 Ablation studies

Table 3 ablates the full OpenWAM method. Token ablations keep the motion gate unchanged; motion ablations keep the token policy unchanged. Request latencies are averaged over complete rollouts. Fixed 2F/4F use fixed evaluation counts with the normal token policy.

Token reuse and selection. Disabling reuse gives 93.8% success at 72.10 ms, compared with 93.4% at 63.76 ms for the full method. Uniformly selecting btb_{t} random positions instead of the RGB/feature-guided set preserves the refreshed token count but lowers the success rate to 91.3%, supporting informative token selection.

Capacity filling. Filling from the minimum refresh budget rtr_{t} to capacity btb_{t} raises the success rate from 92.1% to 93.4%, with request latency increasing from 61.78 to 63.76 ms. First-forward latency rises from 30.76 to 30.96 ms when filling from 65 to 80 tokens (Table 3a).

Motion-adaptive refinement. The motion gate yields 93.4% success at 63.76 ms, versus 91.1% at 64.77 ms for random 2F/4F selection using the original gate’s usage proportions. This supports allocating refinement based on motion. Fixed 2F reaches 89.6% success at 54.70 ms, while Fixed 4F reaches 93.7% at 95.26 ms. The adaptive policy attains a success rate close to Fixed 4F with a lower mean request latency. Appendix E gives paired prediction diagnostics.

Visualization of dynamic allocation. Figure 6 aligns observations, selected evaluation budgets, and token allocation over one complete rollout. Both evaluation budgets and all three token capacities occur.

4.5 Real-world evaluation

Table 4 compares Native and RealtimeWAM on the five tasks in Figure 7 under the same synchronous inference and action execution policy. Average success rates rise from 35.6% to 52.8% on FastWAM and 33.6% to 70.8% on OpenWAM (+17.2 and +37.2 percentage points). Mean inference latency decreases from 210.71 to 23.72 ms and from 640.87 to 65.27 ms, respectively.

5 Conclusion

RealtimeWAM combines parallel execution, hardware-aware token reuse, and motion-adaptive refinement in a training-free framework. On FastWAM and OpenWAM, measured average speedups reach 8.90×\times and 10.67×\times, with success rates within 0.02 and 0.53 percentage points of native inference. Across five real-world tasks, average success rates improve by 17.2 and 37.2 percentage points.

AI use statement

We used generative AI tools to assist with manuscript writing and editing, including improvements to wording, grammar, clarity, and organization, as well as LaTeX formatting. The authors reviewed and revised the AI-assisted content to ensure that it accurately reflects the methods and results. The authors take full responsibility for the accuracy and integrity of the final manuscript.

Appendix A Real-World Setup and Evaluation

A.1 Platforms and tasks

We use a Franka Research 3 robot and a RealSense D435i camera. Figure 8 shows the three setups used for our five tasks. The conveyor runs at 1 m/min for shuttlecock stacking, carrot placement, and tennis-ball placement. The rolling-can task uses an inclined tabletop with one edge raised by 5 cm; mug hanging uses a level tabletop.

A.2 Evaluation protocol

We compare native inference with RealtimeWAM on both FastWAM and OpenWAM. Each task uses 50 trials per backbone and inference configuration, with the same synchronous inference and action execution policy across the comparison. Each inference request predicts a chunk of 32 future actions. The robot executes actions at a control frequency of 20 Hz. Inference runs locally, with negligible network transmission latency. Table 5 lists the task goals; its task IDs match the rollout rows in Figure 7. Table 4 reports success rate and measured mean inference latency; its averages weight the five tasks equally.

In our conveyor experiments, task success was substantially lower when measured inference latency exceeded approximately 90 ms. The dashed line in Figure 1 marks this empirically observed latency threshold.

Appendix B Evaluation Protocols and Detailed Results

B.1 Benchmarks and comparison settings

Benchmarks.

We evaluate FastWAM and OpenWAM on RoboTwin 2.0 (Chen et al., 2025), LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023), and LIBERO-Plus (Fei et al., 2026). RoboTwin Clean and Random are reported separately, giving four settings in Table 1. LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus each report Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long categories; their individual success rates appear in Table 6.

Evaluation protocol.

We use the benchmark environments’ task-success checks. A rollout succeeds if the task goal is satisfied within the evaluation horizon; otherwise it fails. RoboTwin uses 100 rollouts per task in each of its Clean and Random settings. LIBERO uses 50 rollouts per task with the released initial-state sets and goal predicates; Long denotes libero_10. LIBERO-Plus uses one rollout per perturbed task variant, covering changes to layout, cameras, robot initial state, language, lighting, background, and sensor noise (Fei et al., 2026). These protocols apply to both backbones and all methods in Table 1.

Comparison settings.

We use the officially released fine-tuned checkpoints of FastWAM and OpenWAM. For each backbone and evaluation setting, Native, the caching baselines, and RealtimeWAM share the same model weights. All methods use the same evaluation seeds and initial scenes within each backbone and evaluation setting, enabling paired comparisons. Each backbone’s original Native execution provides the reference. VLA-Cache, TeaCache, ToCa, BAC, and RealtimeWAM use compilation and CUDA Graph replay for the main-table latency comparison. The caching baselines retain their original execution schedules, while RealtimeWAM incorporates the proposed parallel execution. Appendix C.3 compares original and compiled execution, including Native. Runtime measurements use BF16, batch size one, and a modified 48 GiB RTX 4090.

B.2 Metrics and aggregation

For an evaluated task or task variant qq, let nqn_{q} be the number of rollouts and yq,i∈{0,1}y_{q,i}\in\{0,1\} the benchmark’s success indicator. Its success rate is SRq=100​nq−1​∑i=1nqyq,i\mathrm{SR}_{q}=100\,n_{q}^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{q}}y_{q,i}. RoboTwin averages task success rates within each setting. LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus average task or task-variant success rates within each category; their main-table scores are the arithmetic means of the four categories. For each setting, latency is the mean of measured request times collected during complete closed-loop rollouts. Each request uses its selected token set and Transformer evaluation budget. The execution comparisons in Tables 2, 7, and 9 use the same rollout-based mean latency definition for each evaluated configuration.

Timing runs from prepared CPU images and robot state to denormalized CPU actions. It includes input processing, model and sampler execution, transfers, and synchronization. Compilation, graph capture, warmup, profiling, and robot execution are excluded.

Tables 1 and 9 average latency equally across the four settings; Table 1 also averages success equally across these settings. Speedup is the original Native average latency divided by the method’s average latency, computed before rounding. Table 3 reports measured first-forward latency (First) and mean request latency over complete rollouts (Request). All latencies are reported in milliseconds.

B.3 Component ablation settings

Table 3 evaluates variants of the full OpenWAM method on RoboTwin. Token ablations keep the motion gate unchanged; motion ablations keep the token policy unchanged.

Token reuse and selection.

w/o token reuse refreshes all observation positions. Random tokens retains the selected execution capacity btb_{t} and uniformly samples that many positions without replacement from all MM positions. w/o capacity filling refreshes rtr_{t} positions instead of btb_{t}, retaining required positions and feature ranking.

Motion gate.

Fixed 2F and Fixed 4F use two and four Transformer evaluations, respectively, within the ten Euler updates. Their token refresh counts follow the observation. Random gate samples between the two budgets using the original motion gate’s usage proportions, independently of predicted motion.

B.4 Category-level benchmark results

Table 6 gives the category-level success rates underlying the benchmark summaries in Table 1. The RoboTwin average combines Clean and Random; each LIBERO or Plus average combines Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long with equal weight.

Appendix C Execution Efficiency

C.1 Execution settings and fixed budgets

Table 2 cumulatively adds CUDA Graph replay, compilation, parallel execution, and token reuse. First starts from CPU images and state and ends after input processing, Prefill, and the first complete predictive evaluation. It includes selection, gathering, cache writes, and stream joins. First is measured in 2F runs; Full 10F uses separate complete requests through denormalized CPU action return. Both report mean wall-clock latency measured during complete closed-loop rollouts, excluding compilation, capture, warmup, and profiling.

Table 7 compares dense execution at two, four, and ten Transformer evaluations within ten Euler updates. Measurements use BF16 on the modified 48 GiB RTX 4090, PyTorch 2.7.1/CUDA 12.8, an Intel Core Ultra 9 285K, four PyTorch threads, and CPU affinity 0–7. OpenWAM’s Native baseline uses commit a8992b613fdb; compilation uses reduce-overhead with verified graph replay. Parallel denotes dependency-aware scheduling and its accompanying runtime optimizations (Section 3.2).

OpenWAM timing begins with composed CPU PIL images and state; FastWAM begins with three RGB arrays and state, including composition and resize. Both include input preparation, VAE and context processing, model evaluations, sampler updates, transfers, synchronization, and CPU action return. Prompt embeddings are warm. Sensor acquisition, communication, robot execution, setup, and output-video decoding are excluded.

At ten evaluations, the Parallel configuration reduces Compile + Graph latency from 450.90 to 223.27 ms on OpenWAM and from 99.68 to 33.52 ms on FastWAM.

C.2 Numerical agreement

Table 8 compares Parallel and Native predictions at matched budgets. FastWAM checks vary state, instruction, images, and noise; direct execution and graph replay agree bitwise on these cases. OpenWAM’s official and modified Native controls also agree bitwise.

C.3 Compiled caching baselines

Table 9 compares original execution with compilation and CUDA Graph replay under the main-table evaluation protocol. Native remains the original implementation when computing main-table speedup.

C.4 Preparation scheduling

The historical OpenWAM step-600 profiling runtime uses BF16 on the 48 GiB RTX 4090 with PyTorch 2.7.1/CUDA 12.8 (snapshot 5f9dede, upstream 898e2f9). It refreshes 80 observation positions, computes all future-video and action positions, and uses two Transformer evaluations within ten Euler updates. Repeated inputs and α=0\alpha=0, ℬ={80,120}\mathcal{B}=\{80,120\} fix the refresh count; online selection and filling still execute. Two observations are each repeated for 50 rounds with three interleaved schedules, restoring dense history and noise before every call. Timing covers composed CPU images/state through CPU actions, including preparation, selection, cache updates, transfers, and waits; restoration and warmup are excluded.

The schedules select identical positions and return bitwise-identical actions. Paired median savings are 0.778 ms for VAE/condition overlap and 0.274 ms for early RGB routing, with round-bootstrap 95% intervals [0.742, 0.822] and [0.225, 0.324] ms.

Appendix D Token Reuse and Selection

D.1 Cache state and feature correspondence

The observation cache stores ungated FFN outputs for 120 positions at each layer. Layer 0 is dense; layers 1–29 share a refresh set. Attention uses current features at every position, and current residual gates apply to fresh and cached FFN outputs. Future-video and action branches are complete at every requested evaluation. Selected cache entries update; others retain their last refreshed outputs. The layer-0 selector reference advances at each observation. Episode boundaries reset history; changes to weights, conditioning, camera layout, or preprocessing require compatible cache state or full refresh.

We compare 14 observation pairs from one FastWAM trajectory and 44 pairs from four OpenWAM adjust_bottle trajectories, eight environment steps apart. FFN change at each token is the channelwise mean absolute or L2 difference between dense features. Mean within-frame RGB/FFN-MAE correlations are 0.827/0.817 for FastWAM/OpenWAM at layer 0 and 0.716/0.701 across layers 1–29. Figures 10 and 11 show typical and weaker correspondence: small RGB changes can accompany larger feature changes. Each model and metric uses the same color range across examples.

For the 44 OpenWAM pairs, a dense-history probe selects the 56 positions with the smallest layer-0 change and compares them with later layers. Change is measured by symmetric relative L1 distance, 2​∥x−y∥1/max⁡(∥x∥1+∥y∥1,10−12)2\lVert x-y\rVert_{1}/\max(\lVert x\rVert_{1}+\lVert y\rVert_{1},10^{-12}). The mean observation-set overlap is 85.4%, versus 46.7% by chance, supporting a shared selection across observation layers.

D.2 Selection at matched refresh counts

Figure 12 compares RGB-guided and random selection on one simulation pair and one real-video pair. Each comparison fixes refresh count, cache history, inputs, noise, and the two Transformer evaluations at updates 0 and 3. Layer 0 and attention remain complete. Action MAE is measured against the same-input dense prediction over the 32-action chunk, using the model’s active normalized coordinates.

Real video.

The tennis-ball pair is sampled at 14.6 and 15.0 s from a 120-fps recording, selected by RGB MAE among candidate pairs 0.4 s apart. An 1800×14401800\times 1440 crop is resized to 320×256320\times 256 in the front-camera slot, with other camera rows fixed black. The step-3,500 OpenWAM checkpoint is fine-tuned on the five robot tasks. Both frames use fixed proprioception from frame 294 of a recorded tennis-ball trajectory, training normalization, and the instruction “Pick up the tennis ball from the conveyor and place it into the bowl.” BF16 feature capture and replay use A100. Guided and 20 random masks each reuse 37 of 80 visible positions plus 40 padded positions. Mean action MAE over ten active coordinates is 0.004866 for guided selection and 0.018892 for random selection (74.2% lower).

Simulation.

The released three-camera FastWAM RoboTwin checkpoint uses transition fast_ep0_obs3 in A100 eager mode. Guided and three random masks each refresh 64 of 120 positions. MAE over 14 normalized joint-action coordinates is 0.004609 for guided selection and 0.018048 for random masks on average (74.5% lower). Full refresh matches dense computation bitwise.

Spatial masks.

Panels a,b use an RGB-only diagnostic rule on the 12×1012\times 10 grid: refresh positions above 5/2555/255 mean absolute RGB change, then protect the top quarter of remaining positions by a camera-local smoothed score. Smoothing uses fourfold downsampling and a Gaussian with standard deviation four and reflected boundaries. These displayed masks reuse 41/120 simulation positions and 37/80 visible real-camera positions. Panel d uses the fixed counts above. The full selector is evaluated through Random tokens in Table 3.

D.3 Capacity filling and recursive reuse

Refresh-count sweep.

Figure 12c uses the historical step-600 OpenWAM profiling runtime on RTX 4090 with two Transformer evaluations. Three observation pairs (frames 1598/1600, 2798/2800, and 3998/4000 of a 30-FPS recording) are evaluated at all 120 refresh counts with five timing rounds per pair. Each call restores dense history and noise. RGB-required positions precede other positions, ranked within each group by layer-0 feature change. The three pairs have 1, 0, and 12 required positions; smaller budgets omit required positions in this fixed-budget diagnostic.

The 3,585 timed calls interleave target counts with an 80-token control. Each point uses the control median plus the median paired latency difference. Timing includes online selection, packing, cache writes, transfers, and waits; restoration, warmup, and error analysis are excluded. Action MAE averages the 32×1032\times 10 normalized action coordinates over three pairs relative to full refresh. That reference has mean MAE 0.00113 against the original dense engine.

Reducing refresh from 120 to 80 changes First from 36.41 to 30.95 ms and Request from 55.94 to 50.36 ms. Within the middle plateau, 32-to-80 filling reduces MAE from 0.00503 to 0.00389 (22.7%), with request latencies 50.71 and 50.36 ms; individual error increments are not monotonic. Table 3a separately marks measured First at 65 and 80 tokens (30.76/30.96 ms). Its Request column contains complete-rollout means (61.78/63.76 ms).

Recursive reuse.

Table 11 covers 44 transitions from four OpenWAM adjust_bottle trajectories. Each starts with full initialization, followed by 11 updates eight environment steps apart. Recursive variants carry cache history and use their own feature anchors. An age cap of two permits at most two consecutive reuses. Errors are measured against dense FFN computation over the normalized 32×2032\times 20 active action chunk. At 64 refreshed positions, an age cap increases mean MAE from 0.002571 to 0.004006; increasing refresh to 96 with the cap gives 0.001596.

Appendix E Motion-Adaptive Refinement

E.1 Sampler and motion score

Shared-prefix continuation.

We integrate the predicted velocity field using Euler updates, following the flow-matching formulation (Lipman et al., 2023). For updates i=0,…,9i=0,\ldots,9, let hi=Embed⁡(xi,si,c)h_{i}=\operatorname{Embed}(x_{i},s_{i},c) be the current latent embedding, with timestep sis_{i} and conditioning cc. Writing BB for the full Transformer, we cache its input-to-output residual

Ci={B⁡(hi,si,c)−hi,i∈ℰ,Ci−1,i∉ℰ.C_{i}=\begin{cases}B(h_{i},s_{i},c)-h_{i},&i\in\mathcal{E},\\ C_{i-1},&i\notin\mathcal{E}.\end{cases} (6)

The output head and Euler update are evaluated at every step:

v~i=Head⁡(hi+Ci,si),xi+1=xi+Δ​ti​v~i.\widetilde{v}_{i}=\operatorname{Head}(h_{i}+C_{i},s_{i}),\qquad x_{i+1}=x_{i}+\Delta t_{i}\widetilde{v}_{i}. (7)

The cache is initialized at update 0 of each request. The 2F schedule uses ℰ2={0,3}\mathcal{E}_{2}=\{0,3\} and the 4F schedule uses ℰ4={0,3,6,9}\mathcal{E}_{4}=\{0,3,6,9\}; the 10F reference refreshes at every update. NFE counts full Transformer evaluations. All schedules share ten Euler updates and fixed observation and instruction conditioning within a request.

After the second Transformer refresh at update 3, we decode a coarse action prediction and measure its amplitude using Equation 5. If refinement is selected, the runtime continues with additional Transformer refreshes at updates 6 and 9, retaining the same initial noise and conditioning. OpenWAM caches the residuals of the future-video and action Transformers; FastWAM caches the action Transformer residual.

Coordinates and threshold.

In the Cartesian-action probes, displacement is the maximum Euclidean distance from current end-effector XYZ across 32 predicted positions, using the training action statistics to restore metres. The joint-action FastWAM runtime obtains XYZ by forward kinematics before evaluating displacement. The recorded RoboTwin motion probes use a fixed 0.08 m threshold; rotation and gripper coordinates do not enter this score.

E.2 Paired prediction comparisons

Deviation is the mean Euclidean XYZ error over both arms and the first 24 predicted steps. Relative deviation divides this error by the largest 10F displacement across those steps and arms, with a 0.02 m floor. Across 93 paired observations from one trajectory each of stack_bowls_two, blocks_ranking_size, and put_bottles_dustbin (18, 49, and 26 requests), we compare 2F and 4F with the same model’s 10F output. Table 12 compares the fixed and adaptive budgets, weighting requests equally. The gate selects 4F for 30 of 93 requests at a coarse 2F displacement threshold of 0.08 m. For these 30 small-motion requests, mean relative deviation is 0.164 with 2F and 0.040 with 4F. For the other 63 requests, the corresponding means are 0.050 and 0.022. The absolute mean reductions are 3.62 mm and 4.14 mm, respectively. The larger relative reduction in the small-motion group partly reflects its smaller normalization denominator; its absolute 2F deviation is also lower.

Figure 13 separates relative and absolute error. Small-motion requests show larger relative deviations under 2F, while the absolute-error view reveals both the role of normalization and variation across requests. Refinement reduces deviation from 10F on 90 of the 93 observations and increases it on the remaining three.

A separate FastWAM replay covers 1,798 observations (Table 13). Four evaluations reduce mean executed-prefix action MAE against the 10F reference from 0.007304 to 0.001224, and P95 from 0.010497 to 0.001713. Fixed-budget comparisons share the observation, initial noise, integration schedule, and action normalization.

E.3 Visualization settings

Figure 3a displays requests 1–25 of the put_bottles_dustbin episode; all 26 requests enter the paired analysis. Predicted speed is end-effector displacement per control step. The display smooths 608 samples with a Gaussian (σ=4\sigma=4 steps, radius 12, reflected endpoints), then retains every fourth sample. The two deviation strips use 2F/4F predictions against 10F, with the relative metric above and a common range of 0–0.25. Images are recorded request inputs. Panel b uses schematic paths and task-tolerance radii.

Figure 6 uses all 50 requests from one OpenWAM blocks_ranking_size rollout. At the 8 cm threshold, 30 requests use 2F and 20 use 4F. Token capacities are 16, 80, and 120, with full initialization. The episode ends in task failure.
